title: Tracking Forms & User Behaviour
description: Tracking valid form-submissions is pretty easy with Google Tag Manager — it’s Form-Submit-listener has a “Check Validation”-setting: Only fire tags if the form will successfully subm
body_html:
Tracking valid form-submissions is pretty easy with Google Tag Manager — it’s Form-Submit-listener has a “Check Validation”-setting:

Only fire tags if the form will successfully submit. If unselected, fire tags whenever a user tries to submit the form.

Unfortunately, this will not work with back-end validated forms, unless the back-end provides information to Google Tag Managers dataLayer upon successful submission.

This is not very generic, and often requires extra back-end work per form — so let’s look at other ways to solve this problem in a more user-friendly and generic way.

In this blog-post, we’ll look into HTML5’s built-in form-validation.
We’ll start with a basic sign-up form (Online example here).:

In order to trigger the browser’s built-in, and thus client-side, form-validation — we need to add some HTML5-attributes to our form’s inputs:

required
This boolean attribute tells the browser that the input-field is required. Some browsers will also match the input’s type upon validating, ie.: “date”, “email”, “number”, “text” etc.

title
The title-attribute provides a tooltip for the input, but it will also be added to some browsers’ validation-message if the input is empty or incorrect.

pattern
The pattern-attribute acts as a regular expression-template for the given input, ie:

<input type="tel" pattern="\d{8}" />

— will match 8 digits.

Mission (almost) accomplished!

But HTML5 has more to offer us. By adding the placeholder-attribute, we can easily show the user how the value is supposed to look like.

And by adding the title-attribute to the input’s label for further information — and beef it up with a little CSS, the odds of the user submitting an incorrect filled-out form are low.

CSS Pseudo-classes

HTML5’s form validation also provides a range of CSS-pseudo-classes:

  • valid
  • invalid
  • required
  • optional
  • in-range
  • out-of-range
  • read-only
  • read-write

—Mixed with SVG background-images (for those wonderful retina-displays!) and an autofocus-attribute for the first input, the form now looks like this (Online example here).:

—and that is without any JavaScript, just pure HTML5 and CSS3!

By checking the “Check Validation”-setting in Google Tag Manager, the form submit-event will now only be fired if the form passes the browser’s built-in validation.

Tracking user behavior

By hacking into the browsers built-in validation through JavaScript, we can track the users’ behavior and thus gain insights into the form’s usability.
Maybe the required password-strucure is too complex? Or something else?

By temporarily by-passing the browsers built-in validation, we will check the validity-object for valid; we’ll ignore empty inputs (valueMissing), but only track inputs that are incorrectly filled out.

Those values will be added to a custom event in Google Tag Manager (excerpt):

for (i = l; i--;) {
  oField = oForm.elements[i];
  if (oField.nodeName !== "INPUT" && oField.nodeName !== "TEXTAREA" && oField.nodeName !== "SELECT") continue;
  if (typeof oField.willValidate !== "undefined") oField.checkValidity();

  if (!oField.validity.valid) {
    // Do not track empty input-fields
    if (!oField.validity.valueMissing) {
      oEvent = 
      {
        "event": "setEvent",
        "eventAction": "formValidationError",
        "eventCategory": oForm.name + "_" + (oField.name || oField.id),
        "eventLabel":  oField.value
      };
      window.dataLayer.push(oEvent);
    }
    break;
  } 
}

—Now, going to Google Tag Manager’s “Behavior > Events”-section, under “formValidationError”, we can look up our form and see precisely which inputs cause problems for the users!

Final example

The final example, including the tracking script is available here (view source/inspect to see the HTML, CSS and JavaScript).

Legacy browsers

It’s only the so-called evergreen-browsers that supports HTML5 forms and it’s CSS pseudo-classes. The forms above will work in IE9 and below, but the validation and styling will be gone.

However, our focus was on enhancing existing (back-end-validated) forms — and by doing these small changes, the user-experience will be significantly better for at least 70% of the users.

But all is not lost for legacy browsers. The H5F-project provides HTML5 form-validation for older browsers — but without behavior-tracking (this would require a customized, re-written version of the H5F-script).

Finally, one could also imagine a script that would add HTML5-validation to existing forms automatically, with a few customizations per client.
